title: Rate limiting
scopeHtml: Scope: fixed and sliding windows, token and leaky bucket, distributed limiter with Redis, headers, 429 and backoff, limit design.

notes.title: Why rate limiting
notes.html:
Rate limiting caps how many requests a caller may make in a time window, so one noisy caller cannot hurt everyone else. It protects against abuse (scrapers, brute-force logins), accidents (a client bug retrying in a tight loop), cost blowups (paid downstream APIs, LLM calls), and overload (it is the first line of load shedding).

Decide three things: who is limited (user id, API key, IP, tenant), what is counted (requests, bytes, cost units), and how the limit behaves (hard reject, queue, slow down).

Worked example. Login endpoint: 5 attempts per minute per account plus 20 per minute per IP. A password-guessing bot at 1,000 tries/s is cut to 5 tries/min per account: 1.7 million guesses per day drops to 7,200.

Industry examples. Stripe (about 100 requests/s per key in live mode, confirm in docs), GitHub (5,000/hour authenticated), Twitter/X (per-endpoint 15-minute windows), Cloudflare and AWS API Gateway (token bucket), Shopify (leaky bucket for REST, cost-based for GraphQL).

Everyday analogy. A nightclub bouncer who lets in a fixed number per minute so the dance floor never gets crushed.

Common interview traps.

  • Not saying what the key is (IP alone punishes a whole office behind one NAT).
  • Treating rate limiting as only abuse defence; it is also capacity protection and fairness.

notes.title: Where to put the limiter
notes.html:
Edge (CDN/WAF), API gateway, service middleware, or per-dependency client-side; layer them.

Place Good for Weak at
CDN / WAF (Cloudflare, AWS WAF) DDoS, IP-level, bots Knows nothing about users or business rules
API gateway (Kong, Envoy, NGINX, AWS API GW) Per-key/per-route quotas, central Another hop, needs shared state
In-service middleware Business rules (per-tenant plans) Duplicated per service
Client side (Android) Being polite, avoiding 429 Cannot be trusted for security

Decision gravity. Starting at the gateway is easy to add and easy to change (two-way door). The limit values themselves are a public contract once partners build on them; lowering them later breaks customers (one-way-ish). Start generous, publish them, tighten with notice.

NGINX example (single node, leaky-bucket-like):

# nginx.conf
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;   # 10m ~ 160k IPs
server {
  location /api/ {
    limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay;
    limit_req_status 429;
  }
}

Industry examples. Envoy has local and global (external gRPC "ratelimit" service backed by Redis) rate limiting; Kong's rate-limiting plugin can use Redis; Netflix's Zuul uses concurrency limits.

Everyday analogy. Airport security: a check at the road in, at the terminal door, and at the gate; each catches different problems.

Common interview traps.

  • Only limiting at the edge; internal callers can still overload a downstream service.
  • Trusting client-side limiting for protection.

notes.title: Fixed window counter
notes.html:
Count requests in fixed clock windows (for example each minute); reject when the count exceeds the limit. The simplest algorithm.

Mechanism: key = user:42:minute:29374200, INCR it, set expiry 60 s, if count > 100 reject.

Problem: the boundary burst. Limit 100 per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00: 200 requests in 2 seconds while "obeying" the limit. Worst case is 2x the limit around each boundary.

window 12:00          | window 12:01
.................[100]|[100]...............
          0:59 -> 1:00  = 200 in ~2 seconds

Pros: O(1) memory (one counter per key), trivial, atomic in Redis. Cons: boundary burst.

When to use. Coarse protection where 2x spikes are tolerable (daily quotas, "1000 per day"). Billing quotas are naturally fixed windows.

Industry examples. GitHub-style hourly quotas, many API key plans ("10,000 calls/month").

Everyday analogy. A bus pass that resets at midnight: ride 10 times at 11:59 pm and 10 more at 12:01 am.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing the 2x boundary burst.
  • Aligning windows to the wall clock so every client resets at the same moment, then stampedes.

notes.title: Sliding window log and sliding window counter
notes.html:
Sliding windows fix the boundary burst by looking at the last 60 seconds from now, not the current clock minute.

Sliding window log: store the timestamp of every request in a sorted set. On each request: remove entries older than now - 60s, count the rest, reject if >= limit, else add this one.

  • Exact. But memory is O(limit) per key: 100 timestamps per user, times 10M users = 1 billion entries, around tens of GB in Redis.

Sliding window counter: keep two fixed-window counters (current and previous) and weight the previous one. estimate = current + previous * (1 - elapsed_fraction_of_current_window)

Worked example: limit 100/min. Previous minute had 80 requests, current minute has 30 so far, and we are 25% into the current minute (elapsed 15 s). estimate = 30 + 80 * 0.75 = 90 so allowed (90 < 100). At 40% through with current = 50: 50 + 80 * 0.6 = 98 allowed; next would make 99... until the estimate hits 100.

Cloudflare reported (2017 blog) this approximation was off by very few requests in practice (about 0.003% of requests wrongly decided in their sample; confirm exact number in their post). Memory: two counters per key.

Redis sorted-set version (log) in Python:

def allow(r, key, limit, window_ms, now_ms, member):
    pipe = r.pipeline()
    pipe.zremrangebyscore(key, 0, now_ms - window_ms)   # drop old
    pipe.zadd(key, {member: now_ms})                     # add this request
    pipe.zcard(key)                                      # count
    pipe.pexpire(key, window_ms)
    _, _, count, _ = pipe.execute()
    return count <= limit

(Pipelines are not a transaction by default; for strict atomicity use a Lua script. Here a rejected request is also recorded, which is stricter than usual; real versions remove it on reject.)

Industry examples. Cloudflare uses a sliding-window counter; Kong's sliding policy and many Redis libraries (redis-cell, rate-limiter-flexible) provide these.

Everyday analogy. Counting how many cups of coffee you drank in the last 24 hours instead of "today since midnight".

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing the log version at huge scale without computing memory.
  • Forgetting to expire keys, so Redis fills with dead users.

notes.title: Token bucket
notes.html:
A bucket holds up to B tokens and is refilled at R tokens per second; each request takes one token; with no token the request is rejected. It allows bursts up to B but enforces an average rate R.

Config example: B = 20, R = 5/s. A quiet client builds up to 20 tokens, can fire 20 requests instantly, then is limited to 5/s steady.

Implementation trick: do not run a timer. Store tokens and last_refill_ts; on each request compute tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - last) * R), then try to take 1. O(1) memory, two numbers per key.

Java sketch (single node):

class TokenBucket {
  private final double capacity, refillPerSec;
  private double tokens; private long last = System.nanoTime();
  TokenBucket(double cap, double rps) { capacity = cap; refillPerSec = rps; tokens = cap; }
  synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
    long now = System.nanoTime();
    tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) / 1e9 * refillPerSec);
    last = now;
    if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
    return false;
  }
}

Pros: allows natural bursts (real traffic is bursty), tiny memory, easy to explain, weighted cost possible (take 5 tokens for an expensive call). Cons: two parameters to tune; a burst can still hit the backend at B at once.

Industry examples. AWS API Gateway and EC2 API throttling, Stripe, Guava RateLimiter (a smoothing token bucket), Resilience4j RateLimiter, Linux tc, Envoy local rate limit.

Everyday analogy. A prepaid card topped up 5 rupees a second to a max of 20: spend a stash quickly, then you are limited to the top-up speed.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up bucket size (burst) and refill rate (sustained).
  • Using a timer thread per bucket instead of lazy refill.
  • Not considering clock skew when the state is shared across machines.

notes.title: Leaky bucket
notes.html:
A leaky bucket is a queue with a hole: requests enter the bucket and leave at a constant rate; if the bucket is full, new requests overflow and are dropped. It smooths traffic into a steady outflow.

Two views:

  • As a queue: bucket = FIFO queue of size B drained at R/s. Output rate is perfectly constant. Good for protecting a downstream that hates bursts (a payment processor at exactly 50 TPS).
  • As a meter: a counter that increases per request and decreases at R/s, reject when above B. This is mathematically the mirror of token bucket (used by NGINX limit_req).

Comparison:

Token bucket Leaky bucket (queue)
Output Bursty up to B Constant R
Latency None added Requests wait in the queue
Use for API quotas, user-facing limits Protecting fragile downstreams, traffic shaping

NGINX burst=20 (without nodelay) delays excess requests to enforce the rate (leaky behavior); with nodelay it serves the burst immediately and then rejects (token-bucket-like).

Worked example. Downstream SMS gateway accepts 100 messages/s. Marketing fires 5,000 messages in one second. Leaky bucket queue of 10,000 drains at 100/s over 50 s, with nothing dropped, rather than a flood of errors.

Industry examples. Shopify REST (bucket 40, leak 2/s, confirm numbers in docs), NGINX, network traffic shapers, Kafka consumers with max.poll.records + pacing.

Everyday analogy. A funnel into a bottle: pour fast, liquid still drips through at the neck's speed; overflow spills.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying token and leaky bucket are identical; their output behavior differs.
  • Queue growth without a cap (memory and latency blow-up).

notes.title: Distributed rate limiting with Redis
notes.html:
With many API servers, a per-server counter allows N times the limit. All servers must consult shared state, usually Redis.

Why not just in-memory? 10 servers each allowing 100/min means the user effectively gets up to 1000/min depending on load balancing.

Requirements for the Redis approach:

  1. Atomicity. Read-modify-write must be one step or two servers both see "99" and both allow. Use INCR (atomic) for fixed windows, or a Lua script (EVAL) for token bucket and sliding window, because Redis runs a script without interleaving other commands.
  2. Expiry. Always EXPIRE/PEXPIRE so idle keys disappear.
  3. Time source. Use Redis TIME inside the script, not each app server's clock, to avoid skew.

Token bucket as a Lua script:

-- KEYS[1] = bucket key; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, cost
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] + t[2] / 1e6
local data = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local ts = tonumber(data[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (now - ts) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then tokens = tokens - tonumber(ARGV[3]); allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(ARGV[1] / ARGV[2] * 1000) * 2)
return {allowed, tokens}

Scale and cost. One Redis node handles roughly 100,000 simple ops/s (more with pipelining). 200,000 API requests/s needs a Redis Cluster sharded by limiter key (hash the user id): 4 to 8 shards, plus replicas. Added latency about 0.3 to 1 ms in the same AZ per request.

Reducing load on Redis.

  • Local pre-check plus periodic sync (approximate): each server keeps a local counter and syncs every 100 ms or after N requests; accepts a small overshoot for far fewer Redis calls.
  • Local token slices: a server leases 50 tokens from Redis at a time.
  • Use only for expensive routes; cheap routes get coarse limits.

Failure behavior (decision). If Redis is down: fail open (allow; availability first, risk of overload) or fail closed (reject; safe but an outage for everyone). Most public APIs fail open with an alert and a local fallback limiter; login/password endpoints often fail closed. Choose per route and document it.

Other hazards. Hot keys (one huge tenant on one shard), race conditions without Lua, replication lag if reading from replicas (always use the primary for counters), memory growth from missing TTLs, and failover losing the last few counts (acceptable).

Industry examples. Stripe describes Redis-based token bucket limiters and separate load shedders; Lyft's ratelimit service (Envoy) uses Redis; Cloudflare uses Memcached/its own edge counters per data center (approximate, eventually consistent); Figma and Discord have blogged Redis-based limiters.

Everyday analogy. Several ticket counters sharing one central ledger. If each kept its own notebook, one person could buy the max from every counter.

Common interview traps.

  • GET then SET (race) instead of atomic INCR or Lua.
  • Putting the limiter in front of Redis failure with no policy for fail open vs closed.
  • Not sharding the limiter keys, making the limiter itself the bottleneck.

notes.title: Rate limit headers and 429 handling
notes.html:
Tell clients the limit, what remains and when to retry, so well-behaved clients self-throttle.

Server response when limited:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 30
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type":"https://api.example.com/errors/rate-limited","status":429,"code":"RATE_LIMITED","detail":"Limit is 100 requests per minute.","retry_after_seconds":30}

Headers:

  • Retry-After: seconds (or an HTTP date). The one clients must honor.
  • RateLimit-*: an IETF draft standard (RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset); many APIs still use X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset (GitHub uses X-RateLimit-Reset as an epoch time; check each API's semantics).
  • Send these on successful responses too so clients can slow down before hitting 429.
  • 429 is the right code for the caller going too fast; 503 is for the server being overloaded overall; 403 for blocked.

Client behavior on Android (OkHttp interceptor):

class RetryAfterInterceptor : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        var response = chain.proceed(chain.request())
        var attempt = 0
        while (response.code == 429 && attempt < 3) {
            val wait = response.header("Retry-After")?.toLongOrNull()
                ?: (1L shl attempt)                       // 1s, 2s, 4s fallback
            val jitter = (0..250).random()
            response.close()
            Thread.sleep(wait * 1000 + jitter)
            response = chain.proceed(chain.request())
            attempt++
        }
        return response
    }
}

(Blocking sleep is acceptable on OkHttp's worker threads in a small interceptor but prefer a coroutine-based retry for UI-driven calls; only retry idempotent requests or those carrying idempotency keys.)

Exponential backoff with jitter: delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)). Jitter stops all clients retrying in lockstep (the "thundering herd"). Example: base 1 s, cap 60 s: attempts wait up to 1, 2, 4, 8 s...

Incident pattern. A client bug retries immediately on 429: the retry itself feeds the limiter, error rate hits 90%, and the downstream is still hammered. Symptom: 429 rate climbing while unique callers stay flat; request-per-caller graph is spiky. Fix with backoff plus jitter, a client-side circuit breaker, and per-client quotas with escalating penalties.

Industry examples. GitHub returns X-RateLimit-* and secondary limits with Retry-After; Twitter/X returns x-rate-limit-reset; Google APIs recommend truncated exponential backoff.

Everyday analogy. A shop assistant says "come back in 30 minutes", not "no". A good customer returns later rather than shouting from the doorway.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning 429 with no Retry-After.
  • Clients retrying instantly or all at the same second.
  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs blindly.

notes.title: Designing limits: keys, tiers and edge cases
notes.html:
Pick the key, the numbers, and the exceptions on purpose.

Keys: user id (best, needs auth), API key, tenant/org, IP (anonymous traffic, but NAT and mobile carrier CGNAT share IPs, so keep IP limits high), device id (spoofable), and combinations (per user per route).

Tiers: free 60/min, pro 600/min, enterprise custom with burst. Store plan limits in config or the DB, cached in the limiter.

Cost-based: weight expensive endpoints (search = 5 tokens, export = 50). GraphQL: compute query cost; GitHub v4 gives 5,000 "points"/hour.

Concurrency limits: besides rate, cap in-flight requests per caller (for example 10); good for slow endpoints (Netflix adaptive concurrency limits).

Load shedding vs rate limiting: rate limiting is per caller fairness; load shedding drops lowest-priority traffic globally when the server is saturated (Stripe's "load shedder": critical vs non-critical, GET vs POST priorities).

Edge cases:

  • Clock and time zone: use UTC and server time.
  • Retries count toward the limit, so sizing needs headroom (about 20%).
  • Allow-list health checks and internal services; do not limit them accidentally.
  • Shadow mode first: log "would have blocked" for a week before enforcing.

Worked example. Public API, 5,000 paying keys averaging 10 req/s, free users 1,000,000 at 0.01 req/s (about 10,000 req/s total). Capacity is 60,000 req/s. Paid limit 50 req/s with burst 100 allows up to 250,000 req/s worst case; that exceeds capacity, so also add a global load shedder.

Decision gravity. Algorithm choice is easy to swap behind the limiter interface (two-way). Key choice and published numbers are hard to change (one-way for customers).

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing limits as if no one ever retries.
  • Per-IP only limits that block an entire college campus or mobile carrier.
  • Forgetting an escape hatch (temporary allow-list for a launch partner).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Rate limiting protects against abuse, bugs, cost and overload; decide the key (user/API key/IP), the unit (requests/cost) and the behavior (reject/queue).
  • Fixed window: simple, O(1), but up to 2x boundary burst. Sliding window log: exact but O(limit) memory. Sliding window counter: weighted blend of two counters, accurate enough and cheap.
  • Token bucket: allows bursts up to B, sustained rate R, lazy refill with two numbers per key. Leaky bucket: constant output rate via a queue, protects fragile downstreams.
  • Distributed: shared Redis with atomic operations (INCR or Lua), TTL on all keys, Redis TIME, shard by key; reduce load with local slices; choose fail-open vs fail-closed per route.
  • Respond with 429 plus Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers; clients use exponential backoff with jitter and retry only idempotent calls.
  • Layer limits (CDN, gateway, service), start in shadow mode, publish numbers, add load shedding for global overload.

questions.subtopic: Why rate limit and what key to use
questions.promptHtml: Why do we rate limit an API, and how do you decide what to limit on?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you see rate limiting as more than abuse defence and whether you think about the key before the algorithm.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I rate limit to stop one caller from hurting everyone else: abuse like password guessing, client bugs that retry in a loop, cost blowups on paid downstream calls, and plain overload. Before the algorithm I pick three things: who is limited (user id, API key, tenant, IP), what is counted (requests, bytes, cost units) and what happens at the limit (reject with 429, queue, slow down). The key matters most: IP alone punishes a whole office behind one NAT.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A limiter is a function allow(key, cost) -> yes/no. Everything else is how that state is stored.

  • Who: authenticated user id is best. API key or tenant for B2B. IP only for anonymous traffic, and keep it generous because NAT and mobile carrier CGNAT put thousands of users behind one address.
  • What: requests per second is the default. Expensive endpoints should cost more tokens (search = 5, export = 50). For GraphQL compute query cost.
  • Behavior: hard reject (429) for APIs, queue for fragile downstreams, delay for smoothing.
  • Why it matters numerically: login limit 5/min per account turns a bot doing 1,000 tries/s (86.4M/day) into 7,200 tries/day per account.
Client -> API gateway -> Rate limiter -> Service -> DB
                              \-> 429 Too Many Requests

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only thinking of abuse; capacity protection and fairness are the other two jobs.
  • IP-only keys that block offices and campuses.
  • Not saying what happens when the limiter itself fails.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 429 and not 503? -> 429 says "you are too fast", 503 says "the server is overloaded"; clients treat them differently.
  2. Where do you put the limiter? -> Layered: CDN/WAF for IP floods, gateway for per-key quotas, service middleware for business rules.
  3. Can the client enforce it? -> Client-side limiting is politeness only; never a security control.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer names an algorithm. The senior answer starts with the key, the unit and the failure behavior, mentions cost-based limits and that the published numbers become a customer contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A partner behind one corporate NAT got blocked by a per-IP limit of 100/min while 400 employees used the app; moving to per-API-key limits fixed it.

questions.subtopic: Fixed window vs sliding window counter
questions.promptHtml: What is the boundary burst problem in a fixed window rate limiter, and how does a sliding window counter fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic algorithm question; checks if you can compute, not only name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A fixed window counts per clock minute and resets at the boundary, so a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00: 200 in two seconds while obeying a limit of 100/min. The sliding window counter keeps the current and previous window counts and estimates current + previous * (1 - elapsed_fraction), so there is no sharp reset and memory is still two counters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fixed window: key user:42:minute:29374200, INCR, EXPIRE 60, reject if count > 100. O(1) memory, atomic, but worst case is 2x the limit around a boundary.

Sliding window counter worked example, limit 100/min, previous window 80:

  • 25% into the minute, current = 30: 30 + 80 * 0.75 = 90 allowed.
  • 40% in, current = 50: 50 + 80 * 0.6 = 98 allowed; at 100 reject. The estimate assumes the previous window's requests were evenly spread, which is slightly wrong but close (Cloudflare reported a tiny error rate, verify exact number).
fixed:   ......[100]|[100]......   200 in ~2 s
sliding: weight(prev) fades from 1.0 to 0.0 across the current window

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not knowing the 2x worst case.
  • Aligning every client to the wall-clock minute so all retry at the same second.
  • Using the exact log version without computing memory (see the log question).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is fixed window fine? -> Daily or monthly billing quotas where 2x spikes are acceptable.
  2. Why not store every timestamp? -> O(limit) memory per key; 100 x 10M users = 1B entries.
  3. How does token bucket compare? -> It allows a declared burst B and a steady rate R, no boundary artifact.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "sliding is more accurate". Senior: computes the estimate, knows the approximation assumption, and picks fixed for quotas and sliding or token bucket for protection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hourly quota reset at :00 made every partner cron job fire at :00 and stampede; jittered start offsets and sliding windows fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
10 API pods share a Redis limiter. Limit is 100 req/min per user. Support reports a bulk-export customer got 380 requests through in one minute. This is the code:

boolean allow(String userId) {
    String key = "rl:" + userId + ":" + (System.currentTimeMillis() / 60000);
    String v = redis.get(key);
    int count = v == null ? 0 : Integer.parseInt(v);
    if (count >= 100) return false;
    redis.set(key, String.valueOf(count + 1));
    redis.expire(key, 60);
    return true;
}
fun allow(userId: String): Boolean {
    val key = "rl:$userId:${System.currentTimeMillis() / 60000}"
    val count = redis.get(key)?.toInt() ?: 0
    if (count >= 100) return false
    redis.set(key, (count + 1).toString())
    redis.expire(key, 60)
    return true
}

Redis CPU is 15%, replication lag is 2 ms. The customer fires 40 parallel requests.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames Redis lag or says "add a lock in the app". A JVM lock does nothing across 10 pods.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is redis the primary or a replica client? Is the client library pooled across threads? Is the 380 spread over pods? Is time taken from pod clocks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a temporary lower per-key cap at the gateway for that customer.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act race: GET then SET is not atomic, 40 parallel calls all read 99; (b) SET overwrites the count with a stale count+1, so concurrent writers lose increments; (c) EXPIRE after SET is a second call; a crash in between leaves a key with no TTL; (d) pod clocks skew the window id.
  4. How I'd verify: Replay 40 parallel calls in a test, watch MONITOR or redis-cli --latency; check key TTL with TTL rl:... for -1 values.
  5. Root cause: Read-modify-write across two network calls. Two pods both read 99, both write 100, both allow.
  6. Fix: Short term: INCR is atomic.
long c = redis.incr(key);
if (c == 1) redis.expire(key, 60);   // better: Lua, so INCR+EXPIRE are one step
return c <= 100;
val c = redis.incr(key)
if (c == 1L) redis.expire(key, 60)
return c <= 100

Long term: a Lua script for INCR plus PEXPIRE and use Redis TIME, not pod clocks. 7. Prevention: A concurrency test with 50 threads asserting never more than the limit, key TTL alert, reading counters only from the primary. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a distributed lock (slow and itself fragile). Not read from replicas for counters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if INCR succeeds but the pod dies before EXPIRE? -> Key lives forever; use a Lua script or SET key 0 EX 60 NX first, then INCR.
  • Fixed-window boundary still allows 2x; fine? -> Depends; move to sliding counter if the downstream cannot take 2x.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" a limiter leak by adding synchronized. It worked in staging with one pod and failed in production with twelve. The post-incident rule: every counter operation must be a single Redis command or script.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames replication lag, suggests a Java lock.
  • Hire: Spots the race, uses INCR, adds TTL.
  • Strong hire: Also spots the missing-TTL window and clock source, proposes Lua and a concurrency test.

questions.contextHtml: Your notification service calls an SMS vendor that accepts exactly 100 messages/s and returns 429 plus a 60-second ban if you exceed it. Marketing sometimes fires 5,000 messages in one second. Today you use a token bucket with B=200, R=100/s in front of the vendor client. Last week a campaign caused two bans, and 3,000 messages failed.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the token bucket not protect you, and what would you use instead?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the bucket size." That keeps a burst allowed and still drops messages, instead of smoothing them.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are messages time-critical (OTP) or bulk (marketing)? Can bulk wait minutes? Does the vendor count per second window or rolling? Is there one sender process or many?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap bucket to B=100 for the bulk path and pause campaigns until the new path ships.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Token bucket allows a burst up to B=200 in one instant, which the vendor treats as over limit; multiple pods each have their own bucket so total is N x 100; the vendor measures a tighter window than 1 s.
  4. How I'd verify: Vendor dashboard timestamps, per-pod send rate metrics, sum across pods.
  5. Root cause: Token bucket output is bursty by design; the downstream needs a constant rate, which is a leaky bucket (queue drained at R).
  6. Fix: Put bulk messages in a queue (Kafka or SQS) and run a drainer at 100/s total, for example one consumer per partition with a shared limiter. 5,000 messages drain in 50 s, nothing dropped. Keep OTP on a separate high-priority queue with reserved capacity (say 30/s of the 100).
  7. Prevention: Alert on queue age, vendor 429 count; load test with a 5,000 burst.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Queues add latency, so OTP must not wait behind marketing. Cap the queue (for example 10,000) and expire stale messages; an unbounded queue just moves the outage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Campaign is 5M messages? -> 14 hours at 100/s; negotiate a higher vendor limit or add a second vendor.
  • Two pods drain; how to share 100/s? -> Single Redis token bucket or partition the quota 50/50.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fintech's bulk statement emails starved OTP SMS because both shared one queue. Splitting by priority and reserving capacity ended the "OTP arrives in 4 minutes" complaints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Shrinks bucket size and retries.
  • Hire: Names leaky bucket or queue and computes the drain time.
  • Strong hire: Adds priority lanes, queue cap, multi-pod sharing and vendor negotiation.

questions.contextHtml:
Public API, limit 100/min per key. A mobile release 4.2 ships at 10:00. By 10:20 the dashboard shows:

429 rate:        4% -> 63%
unique API keys: 18,000 (flat)
requests/s:      3,000 -> 21,000
per-key request histogram: spikes every ~50 ms
backend CPU:     40% -> 95%

The limiter itself is healthy. The 4.2 changelog says "improved network resilience".
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the limit" or "add servers". That feeds the loop and raises cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the client do on 429? Does a rejected request still count against the limit? Do 429s carry Retry-After? Is the retry on idempotent calls only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tighten rejection to be cheap (reject at the gateway before the backend), return Retry-After: 30, and halt the staged rollout of 4.2.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 4.2 retries instantly on 429 (flat unique keys with 7x requests points at retry amplification); retries are synchronized with no jitter (50 ms spikes); the limiter counts rejected requests so clients never escape; a gateway bug.
  4. How I'd verify: Group by user-agent version, check whether 429 volume is concentrated on 4.2, sample one key's request timeline.
  5. Root cause: Immediate retry on 429 with no backoff and no jitter. Each rejected request becomes a new request, multiplying load while the limiter also counts them.
  6. Fix: Short term: server-side Retry-After and a penalty box. Client: honor Retry-After, exponential backoff random(0, min(cap, base*2^n)), max 3 attempts, retry only idempotent calls or those with idempotency keys. Long term: client circuit breaker.
  7. Prevention: Contract test that the client sleeps on 429; canary releases watching 429 per client version.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not raise limits (hides the bug). Do not drop rejected requests from counting silently without thinking: not counting them is correct for a user who obeys, but a hostile client then costs you CPU, so reject cheaply at the edge.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old versions cannot be updated; now what? -> Server-side escalating penalties and edge rejection; force-upgrade flag if available.
  • Why jitter? -> Without it, all clients retry in the same second: a thundering herd.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "resilience" client change retried 5 times with no delay. Under a brief backend blip the retries multiplied traffic 6x and turned a 30-second blip into a 40-minute outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises limit or scales out.
  • Hire: Identifies retry amplification, adds backoff and Retry-After.
  • Strong hire: Segments by client version, halts rollout, mentions idempotency and cheap edge rejection.

questions.contextHtml:
A team built a sliding window log limiter on Redis sorted sets: limit 600 requests/hour per user, ZADD per request. It worked at 200k users. Marketing expects 10M users next quarter, with about 30% active per hour. Redis shows:

used_memory_human: 41G     maxmemory: 64G
evicted_keys: 0  -> 5,200/min
latency p99: 2 ms -> 11 ms

Each sorted-set member is a request id.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate memory at 10M users and propose a fix. What accuracy do you give up?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just buy a bigger Redis." The memory is O(limit x users) and grows linearly, and evictions silently drop limiter state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is exactness legally required (billing) or is protection enough? Average requests per active user per hour? Is a burst allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise maxmemory temporarily, and shorten the member (store only timestamp integer plus a small suffix) to buy headroom.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Evictions mean the working set exceeds memory; the log is the cause. Check per-key size with MEMORY USAGE.
  4. How I'd verify: MEMORY USAGE rl:u:123, INFO memory, count keys. Math: 3M active x up to 600 entries x about 50 B/entry = 90 GB worst case. Fixed window counter: 3M x ~100 B = 0.3 GB.
  5. Root cause: Exact log memory is O(limit) per key, which scales with users and with the limit.
  6. Fix: Switch to sliding window counter (two integers per key) or token bucket (tokens plus timestamp in a hash, via Lua). Memory drops about 300x. Accuracy cost: the estimate assumes even spread in the previous window; a few requests of error near the limit.
  7. Prevention: Capacity estimate in the design doc; alert on evicted_keys > 0 for the limiter cluster; TTL on all keys.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keep the exact log only for the few endpoints with billing impact. Do not run a limiter on an instance with an eviction policy that evicts live counters silently; use noeviction or a dedicated instance.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Migration without downtime? -> Dual-run the new algorithm in shadow mode, compare decisions for a week, then switch.
  • Limit rises to 10,000/hour? -> The log grows 16x again; another reason for counters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A limiter and a cache shared one Redis; the log limiter's memory growth evicted cache keys, the DB took the load, and the "rate limiter" caused a database outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scale up Redis.
  • Hire: Computes memory, chooses sliding counter or token bucket.
  • Strong hire: Notes eviction hazard, shadow migration, exact log only where needed.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a token bucket works and how you implement it without a timer thread per bucket.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most common production algorithm; the lazy refill trick separates people who have built one.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at R per second. Each request takes a token; no token means reject. B is the burst size and R is the sustained rate. I do not run a timer: I store tokens and last_ts, and on each request compute tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - last) * R) then try to take one. Two numbers per key, O(1).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example B=20, R=5/s: a quiet client accumulates 20 tokens, fires 20 requests at once, then gets 5/s. Weighted cost is natural: an export takes 50 tokens. Single-node code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class TokenBucket {
  private final double cap, rate; private double tokens; private long last = System.nanoTime();
  TokenBucket(double cap, double rate) { this.cap = cap; this.rate = rate; tokens = cap; }
  synchronized boolean tryAcquire(double cost) {
    long now = System.nanoTime();
    tokens = Math.min(cap, tokens + (now - last) / 1e9 * rate);
    last = now;
    if (tokens < cost) return false;
    tokens -= cost; return true;
  }
}
class TokenBucket(private val cap: Double, private val rate: Double) {
    private var tokens = cap
    private var last = System.nanoTime()
    @Synchronized fun tryAcquire(cost: Double = 1.0): Boolean {
        val now = System.nanoTime()
        tokens = minOf(cap, tokens + (now - last) / 1e9 * rate)
        last = now
        if (tokens < cost) return false
        tokens -= cost; return true
    }
}

nanoTime is monotonic, so wall-clock jumps cannot refill the bucket. In a shared store use the store's clock.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing B (burst) with R (sustained).
  • A timer thread per bucket: 1M buckets, 1M timers.
  • Using wall clock (currentTimeMillis), then a clock step grants a free refill.
  • Forgetting that the burst B still hits the backend at once.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Token vs leaky bucket? -> Token allows bursts, output bursty; leaky queue gives a constant output rate and adds latency.
  2. How do you make it distributed? -> Store tokens and ts in a Redis hash and run the refill-and-take in a Lua script.
  3. B=20, R=5, client idle 1 hour then sends 100 at once? -> 20 pass, the rest rejected; the tokens never exceed B.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: describes the bucket metaphor. Senior: lazy refill, monotonic clock, weighted cost, and says which backends can tolerate burst B.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A limiter using currentTimeMillis let a whole fleet through during an NTP step; switching to monotonic or Redis TIME fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you build a rate limiter that works across 20 API servers, and what do you do when the limiter store is down?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks atomicity, scaling the limiter itself and an explicit failure decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Per-server counters give N times the limit, so all servers consult shared state, usually Redis. Updates must be atomic: INCR for fixed windows, a Lua script for token bucket or sliding window, with Redis TIME as the clock and a TTL on every key. Shard keys across a Redis Cluster since one node does roughly 100k ops/s. If Redis is down I decide per route: fail open with a local fallback limiter for general APIs, fail closed for login and money paths, and alert either way.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Scale: 200k API req/s needs 4 to 8 shards by user hash plus replicas; added latency about 0.3 to 1 ms in-AZ. To cut load: local pre-check with sync every 100 ms, or lease token slices (a pod takes 50 tokens at a time), and limit only expensive routes precisely.

Client -> LB -> API pod -> Redis cluster (shard = hash(user_id))
                   \-> local fallback limiter (if Redis times out)

Failure rules: timeout the limiter call at about 5 to 10 ms so it cannot stall requests; use a circuit breaker; count fail-open events. Read counters from the primary only. Failover can lose a few counts; acceptable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- Redis Lua: atomic take of one token
local t = redis.call('TIME'); local now = t[1] + t[2]/1e6
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(d[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (now - ts) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
local ok = 0
if tokens >= 1 then tokens = tokens - 1; ok = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120000)
return ok

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• GET then SET instead of INCR or Lua.
  • No decision on fail open or closed, so the first Redis blip becomes an incident.
  • Limiter shares an instance with the cache.
  • Hot key: one huge tenant pinning one shard.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fail open vs closed for login? -> Closed or a tight local limit; failing open invites brute force.
  2. How reduce Redis calls 10x? -> Token slices or periodic sync; accept small overshoot.
  3. Multi-region? -> Per-region limits with a share of the global quota, or async sync of counts; strict global limits cost cross-region latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use Redis with INCR". Senior: Lua atomicity, own clock, sharding math, local fallback, per-route failure policy, and the limiter's own SLO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Redis failover took the limiter down; the gateway failed closed for everything and caused a 4-minute total outage for a protection layer.

questions.contextHtml: Your PM says: "We are opening the API to partners next month. Add rate limiting so nobody can take us down." Facts you find: capacity is about 60,000 req/s at 70% CPU. Today 5,000 paying customers average 10 req/s each (50,000 req/s in total), plus ~10,000 req/s from free users. There is no published limit, no API keys per partner yet, and some partners sit behind corporate NATs.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks "100 per minute per IP" with no questions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What do partners contractually expect? Are there tiers (free, pro)? Is traffic bursty (batch jobs at midnight)? Which endpoints are expensive? What is the failure we most fear: abuse, bugs, or capacity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship shadow mode first: log "would block" per key for a week, enforce nothing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The numbers show paid keys at 10 req/s average. A limit of 50 req/s with burst 100 for 5,000 keys allows 250,000 req/s worst case, above capacity of 60,000, so per-key limits alone do not protect the system.
  4. How I'd verify: Histogram of per-key p99 req/s from logs; check whether the top 20 keys dominate.
  5. Root cause of the risk: Per-caller fairness is not global protection.
  6. Fix (design): Key = API key (IP only for anonymous, kept high). Token bucket with plan limits (free 60/min, pro 50/s with burst, enterprise custom) stored in config and cached. Cost weights for expensive routes. A concurrency cap per key (for example 10 in flight). Plus a global load shedder that drops lowest-priority traffic when CPU passes 80%. Return 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers on every response.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards on 429 rate per key, an allow-list escape hatch for launch partners, runbook for temporary raises.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The numbers become a public contract; start generous and tighten with notice, since lowering later breaks customers. The algorithm is easy to swap behind the interface; the key and published limits are not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A partner hits the limit daily; what now? -> Sell a higher tier or batch endpoint, not a silent exception.
  • Retries counted? -> Yes; leave about 20% headroom.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team enforced 60/min on day one with no shadow phase. A partner batch job at 100/min broke their nightly sync and became an executive escalation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks a number without questions.
  • Hire: Asks about keys, tiers, expensive routes; proposes token bucket and headers.
  • Strong hire: Shows the capacity math, adds load shedding, shadow mode and the contract aspect.

questions.contextHtml:
Your limiter is a 6-shard Redis Cluster sharded by tenant_id. At 14:05 API latency for all tenants rises. You see:

shard-3: cpu 100%, ops/s 118k, p99 18 ms
shard-1,2,4,5,6: cpu 35%, ops/s ~40k, p99 0.6 ms
top key on shard-3: rl:tenant:7781  (~95k ops/s)
gateway log: limiter timeout 10ms -> failing open

Tenant 7781 is a new enterprise customer running a load test. Redis memory is fine and there was no failover.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and say what failing open means here.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more shards." Adding shards does not split one key.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 7781's traffic legitimate? What is its plan limit? Do we have tenant-level overrides? Is the fail-open alarm firing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move tenant 7781 enforcement to a local per-pod limiter (limit/N) or slice tokens, and reject the excess at the edge. Rate limit the tenant at the CDN too.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hot key on one shard (matches ops/s per key); big Lua script cost; a client retry storm (check 429 share). Red herring: memory and failover are healthy.
  4. How I'd verify: redis-cli --hotkeys (needs LFU policy) or MONITOR sample, per-tenant request counts at the gateway.
  5. Root cause: One tenant's keyspace = one shard; 95k ops/s of a ~100k ops/s node.
  6. Fix: Short term local token slices: each pod leases 100 tokens from Redis, so Redis ops drop about 100x for this tenant. Long term: split big tenants into sub-keys (tenant:7781:bucket:{0..7}, each with limit/8) or run the check in-process with periodic sync.
  7. Prevention: Alert on per-key ops/s and per-shard imbalance, and a load-test policy for partners.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sub-keys give approximate limits (a tenant can be unlucky and get rejected at 7/8 usage). Failing open protected availability but left the platform unprotected for the duration; for this route it was right, with the alert.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tenant is hostile, not a load test? -> Block at the WAF by key or IP before it reaches the limiter.
  • Can you avoid Redis for the hot tenant? -> Yes, local limiter with limit/N when pod count is stable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single mobile-ad partner generated 80% of limiter ops. After slice leasing, Redis ops dropped from 100k to 3k per second with no visible change in enforcement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scale out Redis.
  • Hire: Identifies hot key; local slicing or sub-keys.
  • Strong hire: Explains fail-open consequence, accuracy trade-off, edge blocking.

questions.contextHtml: Your API has had no limits for 3 years. Traffic is 25,000 req/s with 40,000 active keys. A runaway client caused a 9-minute outage, so leadership wants 100 req/s per key within 2 weeks. You suspect some keys exceed 100 req/s legitimately. You also have a token bucket library but no per-key data.
questions.promptHtml: How do you roll this out without breaking customers?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Turn it on at 100 req/s everywhere on a Tuesday morning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which customers are contractually unlimited? Are there batch partners? Is the outage cause one bad client or general load?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Deploy a coarse, very high safety limit now (for example 1,000 req/s per key) which only catches runaways like the one that caused the outage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A few heavy keys need higher tiers; some traffic is a single user via a shared key; retries inflate counts.
  4. How I'd verify: Shadow mode: compute decisions, log would_block with key, route and count; for 7 days. Aggregate p99 per key.
  5. Root cause of risk: Enforcing blind turns an unknown distribution into customer errors.
  6. Fix (rollout): Week 1 shadow plus headers (RateLimit-*) so clients can see numbers; email the keys that would be blocked, with 30 days notice. Week 2 enforce for keys under the limit with room, grandfather heavy keys with custom tiers. Enforce by percentage (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) with a kill switch. Keep Retry-After on 429.
  7. Prevention: Per-key dashboards, a documented request process for higher limits, release notes with numbers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Published numbers are a contract, and lowering them later breaks customers, so start at the generous end. Not enforce on health checks or internal callers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 5 keys need 400 req/s? -> Custom tier or batch endpoint; record exceptions in config, not code.
  • Kill switch fails? -> Config-driven flag cached locally; test it in drills.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Shadow mode revealed that 60% of "would block" volume came from one SDK retrying on timeouts; fixing the SDK removed the problem before enforcement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Enforces immediately.
  • Hire: Shadow mode, gradual enforcement, notice.
  • Strong hire: Safety limit first, grandfathering, kill switch, headers and SDK analysis.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. Black Friday, 09:12 to 09:40: checkout API errors hit 38%. Facts: a per-IP limit of 60/min at the CDN returned 429 to a large college campus (4,000 students on one NAT) and to a mobile carrier CGNAT range. Separately, an internal recommendation service called the cart service at 9,000 req/s with a bug, saturating its DB; that traffic never crossed the CDN. Gateway per-key limits were healthy. The CDN 429s were 12% of the errors; the cart DB saturation was 26%.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: what went wrong and what is the corrected limiter design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the IP limit" and stop. That ignores the larger internal failure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Timeline of both issues? Did CDN 429s correlate with checkout drop? Why did the internal call bypass limits? Who owns the cart service SLO?
  2. Immediate mitigation (as done): Raise or disable the per-IP rule at the CDN for known carrier ranges, throttle the recommender, scale the cart DB read path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two independent causes: (a) keying on IP at the edge, which is shared by many users; (b) no limit on internal east-west callers; the red herring was the CDN 429 volume, which was the more visible but smaller share.
  4. How I'd verify: Joined logs: 429 by source ASN and user id, per-caller request rate at the cart service, DB connection saturation.
  5. Root cause: One layer was assumed to cover all callers. Edge limits cannot know users; internal callers need their own protection.
  6. Fix: Layered design: CDN/WAF for floods with a high IP threshold and allow rules for NAT-heavy ranges; gateway per-user/API key token buckets; service-level per-caller quotas and concurrency limits (10 in flight) on cart; client-side limiting in the recommender as politeness; a load shedder on cart to drop low-priority traffic.
  7. Prevention: Shadow mode before enforcing new rules, per-layer dashboards, game-day with a runaway internal caller.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not remove IP limits (they stop real floods); do not trust client-side limiting as security. Each layer adds a hop and config to keep consistent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you tell NAT from a botnet? -> Per-user ids behind the IP, challenge (CAPTCHA) rather than hard block, ASN reputation.
  • Who owns limits? -> The service owner sets per-caller quotas; platform owns the mechanism.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A campus IP block cost a retailer launch-day sales from a whole university; a rule review checklist now asks "who shares this key?".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only fixes the IP limit.
  • Hire: Separates the two causes and proposes layers.
  • Strong hire: Adds concurrency caps, load shedding, shadow rollout and ownership.
